issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies imply a current external danger/assault-style threat context (arming oneself, hypervigilant scanning for physical threat) that is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, where danger is usually medical and not mitigated by carrying a weapon or scanning for attackers.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: Within the profile, these threat-focused safety behaviours are not supported by any Threat items and fit poorly with the formulation, which has Triggers and Threat fully inactive; they suggest a strong trigger/threat loop that the rest of the self-report does not reflect.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: The contamination appraisal is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness. It is more characteristic of interpersonal/sexual trauma or moral injury and lacks support from the other selected items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoiding medical cues is plausible for a child's severe illness, but the additional strategies of avoiding public transport and constantly scanning for external threat suggest a danger-based trauma context not represented in the memory or appraisal items.

issues.item: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: For trauma centered on a child's life-threatening illness, avoiding public transport is hard to link clinically unless other items indicate transport-related reminders or hospital-travel cues; no such trigger or memory content is present here, so this strategy appears context-mismatched.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: Constantly scanning the environment for threat implies an ongoing external danger focus, but the rest of the profile is dominated by trauma-memory disorganisation and self-change appraisals rather than current external-threat concerns. With Threat and Trigger links inactive, this item sits awkwardly in the formulation.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: This item is hard to reconcile with the trauma type (child's life-threatening illness) and the rest of the profile. The selected appraisals and memory items center on traumatic recollection, permanent change, and distrust, but not on a current external danger context. 'Constantly scan environment for signs of threat' implies hypervigilance for immediate environmental threat, which is more characteristic of assault/combat-type trauma and is not clinically linked here given that all Triggers and Threat edges are inactive in the formulation. It also sits poorly with the other maladaptive strategies, which are illness/trauma-processing related (avoid care, suppress thoughts).

vignette: Kiet's eyes still welled up with tears whenever he thought about his granddaughter's near-fatal illness. It had been two years since the hospital ordeal, but the memory of her tiny body hooked up to machines and tubes felt more real than any ordinary day that followed. As a nanny, Kiet had always been fiercely devoted to his family; now, the trauma had left him questioning everything he thought he knew about himself. He couldn't shake off the feeling that he had permanently changed for the worse – that he was no longer the same person who used to care for his loved ones with such ease and confidence. Kiet's mind often wandered back to those harrowing days, replaying every conversation with doctors, every beeping of machines, every cry from his granddaughter. He tried hard not to think about it, but the memories lingered, refusing to fade into the background like ordinary recollections. When they did surface, Kiet found himself lost in a world that felt more present than past – as if he was still standing beside his granddaughter's hospital bed, watching helplessly as she struggled to breathe. His inability to make sense of those events, to tell a clear story even to himself, had taken a toll on Kiet's self-perception. He saw himself as unrecognisable, someone who had lost control and couldn't regain it. This distorted view seeped into his relationships; he began distrusting others, wondering if they were hiding something behind their sympathetic smiles and words of encouragement. People, in general, seemed less genuine to Kiet now – even those closest to him. As a result, Kiet started avoiding anything that might trigger more painful memories or feelings of vulnerability. He stopped attending family gatherings, citing exhaustion from his nanny job as an excuse. At work, he became increasingly withdrawn, struggling to connect with the children in his care. His usual warmth and playfulness had given way to distraction – he kept himself occupied all the time, whether it was tidying up toys or scrolling through his phone. Kiet's avoidance extended to medical care; he stopped going for regular check-ups, fearing that doctors might detect some underlying condition that would only add to his anxiety. This decision weighed heavily on him, but Kiet rationalised that seeking help would be a sign of weakness – a confirmation that he had indeed changed for the worse. When memories of his granddaughter's illness resurfaced, as they often did, Kiet tried to suppress them, redirecting his thoughts towards more mundane concerns. Yet, these attempts at mental distraction only seemed to reinforce the loop of negative appraisals and traumatic memories. The more Kiet pushed away his emotions, the more convinced he became that people were not what they seemed – that even his own family might be hiding something from him. His memories, in turn, grew more vivid, as if feeding off his anxiety. It was this vicious cycle that finally brought Kiet to seek help – a reluctant admission that he needed guidance to navigate the darkness that had consumed him. For Kiet, therapy represented a daunting prospect – an invitation to confront the very fears and doubts he had tried so hard to suppress. But with each passing day, his need for answers grew stronger than his avoidance. He hoped that by facing his demons head-on, he might rediscover the person he once was – or, at the very least, learn to live with the person he had become.
